title: On the cryptographic potential of single-qubit rotations
authors: Alex B. Grilo, Lucas Hanouz, Anne Marin
abstract: In the domain of quantum communication, cryptographic protocols often require users to have access to trusted qubit sources or detectors. Recently, it was shown that on an architecture called the Qline, several protocols can equivalently be performed by parties capable only of single-qubit rotations. In this work, we introduce two composably secure constructions that together show how in most quantum cryptographic protocols, parties traditionally required to perform trusted qubit preparation or measurement can delegate these tasks to an untrusted provider and instead rely on a trusted single-qubit rotation device. Our first construction implements single-qubit measurement and is universally applicable across any context. In contrast, our second construction, which addresses qubit preparation, relies on specific assumptions regarding the underlying protocol. We show, however, that these assumptions are inherently satisfied by the vast majority of common quantum cryptographic protocols. A notable consequence of our results is the formal validation of the Qline as a versatile architecture capable of supporting a wide range of single-qubit protocols.
summary: The paper demonstrates that many quantum cryptographic protocols do not require direct access to trusted qubit sources or detectors. Instead, they can be securely re-engineered to function using only a device capable of performing arbitrary single-qubit rotations on the Qline architecture. This significantly simplifies hardware requirements and validates the versatility of rotation-based quantum communication channels.
main_problem: To show that most quantum cryptographic protocols requiring trusted qubit preparation or measurement can be re-engineered to rely only on a trusted single-qubit rotation device.
main_result: The work establishes composably secure constructions demonstrating that the Qline architecture, relying solely on single-qubit rotations, is sufficient to support a wide range of quantum cryptographic tasks.
method: Security proofs are established by showing the indistinguishability ($\approx_0$) between protocols using ideal trusted components and those implemented using only single-qubit rotation devices coupled with untrusted sources/detectors.
model_or_system: The primary model is the Qline architecture, which constrains operations to single-qubit rotations. The analysis covers cryptographic primitives like state distribution for measurement and preparation.
key_observables: Composably secure implementation of quantum tasks; indistinguishability ($\approx_0$) between simulated and actual protocols.
important_parameters: The security advantage $\epsilon$; the underlying protocol structure (e.g., QKD, QOT).
main_assumptions: The constructions assume a trusted single-qubit rotation device; specific assumptions are made about the decomposability of the original protocols.
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the setup for state distribution systems ($S_{DC}$ vs $S_{DB}$) and the structure of the simulator used in security proofs.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first proving secure replacement for single-qubit measurement (Theorem 1), then tackling qubit preparation using CNOT gates (Theorem 2), and finally generalizing to entanglement-based scenarios (Theorem 3) for broader applicability.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful resource-reduction technique, showing that complex quantum protocols can be simplified by standardizing the required hardware trust model around basic single-qubit operations, which is highly relevant for building scalable quantum networks.
